terms.gloss: present, current (as against past or future)
evidence: Gell. 1.10.4: loquere verbīs praesentibus, words now in use (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BC 1.52: inopiā praesentis, sed etiam futūrī temporis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of the speaker’s own time Latin rarely uses praesēns alone, and says hic instead (Lewis & Short): hōc tempore, at the current time.

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 154: quondam … hōc tempore
terms.comment: The current year is hic annus; currently, hōc tempore or nunc (see now).

terms.gloss: current, in general use (of words and customs)

evidence: Cic. Phil. 4.7: ex hodiernō ejus ēdictō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of this very day; the wider sense “present-day” is rare and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short), and Morgan–Owens’s examples are Tertullian’s.

phrases.latin: vīve ergō mōribus praeteritīs, loquere verbīs praesentibus
phrases.english: live, then, by the ways of the past, but speak the words of the present

phrases.latin: adnotābant seniōrēs, quibus ōtiōsum est vetera et praesentia contendere
phrases.english: the older men, who have time to compare past and present, remarked

hic.against: Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel
hic.html: De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke.
